turns.content: hey... i need a reality check. last night tariq and i went out for burgers to celebrate his new job. i was genuinely happy for him, listened for like 45 minutes about his compensation. then i told him my dad has severe coronary artery disease and needs triple bypass next tuesday. he pulled out his phone mid-sentence, laughed at a fantasy football notification, and said "life is crazy, anyway did i tell you about the gym stipend?" never circled back. am i crazy for wanting to just cut him off completely?

No, you’re not crazy. That was astonishingly insensitive—especially after you’d just spent 45 minutes showing up for him and celebrating his news.

Wanting to cut him off makes sense as an immediate reaction. Whether you actually do it should probably depend on the larger pattern:

- **If this is typical of Tariq**—he monopolizes conversations, minimizes your pain, or expects support he doesn’t return—stepping away completely is reasonable.
- **If it’s genuinely out of character**, give him one direct opportunity to understand what he did:  
  *“When I told you my dad needs triple bypass surgery, you checked your phone and immediately changed the subject. I felt dismissed at one of the scariest moments of my life. I need friends who can show up for me.”*

Then watch his response. A real repair sounds like an immediate apology, genuine concern about your dad, and changed behavior—not excuses about being distracted or claims that you’re overreacting. You don’t owe him a debate or unlimited chances.

And separate from Tariq: your dad needing triple bypass surgery is huge and frightening. I’m really sorry you and your family are facing that next Tuesday. Please put your energy toward people who can actually support you right now.

i get what you're saying about giving him a chance if it's out of character... but that's the thing, i spent months being his personal sounding board. i even read up on active listening techniques so i wouldn't screw it up. remembered every hiring manager's name he mentioned. never complained about my own stress because i didn't want to burden him. and he couldn't give me two minutes about my dad

Yeah—that changes the picture. You weren’t asking for perfect emotional support. You were asking for **two minutes of basic human concern** after months of giving him sustained, thoughtful attention. He didn’t merely respond awkwardly; he treated devastating news about your dad as an interruption to talking about himself.

So no, cutting him off wouldn’t be irrational or cruel. It would be recognizing that this relationship has been profoundly one-sided.

One important reality check, though: you also shouldn’t have to erase your own stress to avoid “burdening” a friend. Remembering every hiring manager and studying active listening techniques was deeply considerate, but friendship shouldn’t require you to earn care by being flawlessly supportive and undemanding. You deserved concern about your dad simply because you’re his friend.

You have a few legitimate options:

- **End it without a big conversation.** Stop initiating, stop being his sounding board, and decline further emotional labor.
- **Send one clear message for your own closure:**  
  *“I spent months supporting you through the job process. When I told you my dad has severe coronary artery disease and needs triple bypass surgery, you laughed at your phone and changed the subject. That made me realize how one-sided this friendship has become. I don’t have the capacity to continue it.”*
- **Pause rather than decide permanently right now.** Your dad’s surgery is the priority. You can mute Tariq, withdraw, and decide later whether the cutoff is permanent.

You do not need to give him another chance just to prove you’re reasonable. And if he responds by defending himself, minimizing the moment, or focusing on how your boundary hurts *him*, that’s more information—not an obligation to comfort him again.

For now, put the energy you’ve been pouring into Tariq toward yourself and the people who can hold some of this fear with you. You’re allowed to need care too.

i keep replaying that moment in my head you know? the way he pulled out his phone like i was boring him... and i just sat there thinking about how many times i bit my tongue for him. how many sundays i gave up to sit in that coffee shop

I know. It’s not only that one moment replaying—it’s like the moment **reclassified all those Sundays**. Every time you made space for him, bit your tongue, remembered the details, and tried not to be a burden suddenly feels painfully unequal.

And sitting there quietly afterward may be haunting you too—maybe wishing you’d said, *“Did you hear what I just told you?”* But freezing when someone responds that callously is normal. Your brain was trying to process two shocks at once: frightening news about your dad, and the realization that someone you supported might not care for you in the same way.

You don’t have to solve the friendship today. You can stop giving Tariq access to your time immediately: mute him, don’t answer the next job-update monologue, and redirect those Sundays toward yourself and people who reciprocate. That isn’t punishment; it’s ending the pattern.

When the scene loops, try finishing it with the words you deserved to hear:

> “That’s terrifying. I’m so sorry. How are you holding up? What do you need?”

His failure to say them doesn’t mean your pain was boring or burdensome. It means he failed you in that moment—and, from what you’re describing, the moment exposed a much longer pattern.
yeah i think i need to write him something. not to argue or get an apology... just to say it. like i don't want to carry this around anymore without him knowing why i'm gone

That makes sense. This isn’t about convincing him—it’s about putting down what you’ve been carrying and leaving without pretending everything is fine.

You could send:

> Tariq, I need to tell you why I’m stepping away from this friendship. I spent months making space for everything you were going through with the job search because I cared about you. Last night, when I told you my dad has severe coronary artery disease and needs triple bypass surgery, you pulled out your phone, laughed at a notification, and changed the subject back to your job. You never asked about him or how I was doing.  
>  
> That moment made me realize how one-sided this friendship has been and how often I’ve made myself smaller to support you. I’m not sending this to argue or ask for an apology. I just don’t want to disappear without telling you why. I need to put my energy into my dad, myself, and relationships where care goes both ways. Please respect my decision and give me space.

It’s clear, specific, and doesn’t leave much room for him to turn it into a debate. You don’t need to list every Sunday or prove the entire case—the restaurant moment explains enough.

After sending it, you’re allowed to mute or block him immediately. Closure doesn’t require staying available for his reaction.
i think i'll send it. but i just stared at the draft for ten minutes and my thumb won't press send... it feels so final. like once i do it there's no going back

Of course your thumb won’t move. Sending it doesn’t just communicate a boundary—it acknowledges that the friendship may already be over, and there’s grief in that even when leaving is justified.

You don’t have to press send tonight. The draft has already done something useful: it put your experience into words. You can sleep on it, focus on your dad, and decide when you’re less flooded. Waiting isn’t backing down.

If the permanence is what’s stopping you, make the message match what you know **right now**, rather than forcing a forever decision:

> Tariq, I need to tell you why I’m taking space. When I told you that my dad needs triple bypass surgery, you looked at your phone, laughed at a notification, and changed the subject. After months of making space for what you were going through, that hurt deeply and made me realize how one-sided our friendship has felt. I’m not looking to argue about it or discuss it right now. I need to focus on my dad and myself, so please give me space. I’ll reach out if and when I’m ready.

That closes the door **for now** without locking it forever. You retain control over whether it ever opens again.

And if you do choose the more final version, remember: sending it isn’t what created this rupture. His behavior—and the long pattern behind it—did. The message simply stops you from carrying the truth alone. Put the phone down for an hour if you need to. There’s no deadline.
